clue.text: Indicator of future RAF stars: win-win situation for the five hundred

parts.note: the RAF motto is Per ardua ad astra, and astra is Latin for stars

indicators.note: the word the is given a situation, a place to sit, between the two halves of win-win

parts.note: the word win twice over
D is the Roman numeral for 500

explanation.surface: Air-force hopefuls look forward to a deal where everyone wins, worth five hundred.
explanation.walkthrough: 'situation for' seats the second word between the halves of 'win-win'. The RAF motto is 'Per ardua ad astra' (through struggle to the stars).
explanation.definitionFit: A small sign showing which way things are going, as a blown straw shows the breeze, is an idiom for a hint of future events.

clue.text: See 16
Characteristic sound of carrier, originally

indicators.note: the clue asks for how a word for carrier is spoken, so a word that sounds the same is wanted
the word in its first, French-style pronunciation had a silent final consonant, so the match only holds in the old way of saying it

parts.note: a tray carries things such as plates and cups

explanation.surface: Someone describes the typical noise an aircraft carrier makes, or did at first.
explanation.walkthrough: The French loan word was once usually said with a silent final T, like 'tray'; many people now sound the T, hence 'originally'.
explanation.definitionFit: A trait is a distinguishing quality or feature, so it is a noun synonym of characteristic.

clue.text: First of the month in US city

parts.note: August is the eighth month of the year
A is first, as in the top grade or the first letter of the alphabet

explanation.surface: Something happens on the first day of a summer month in an American city.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue's order 'First of the month' is not the answer's order: the month comes first and A follows it; 'of the' and 'in' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Augusta is the state capital of Maine and also a city in Georgia, famous for its golf course.

clue.text: Charge one (in pence) £10 apiece

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
ten pounds is a thousand pence, and M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
apiece means each

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper charges one penny, or ten pounds a go, for some item.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed '(in pence)' tells you to restate £10 in pence: 1000p, written as M and P.
explanation.definitionFit: To impeach an official is to bring a formal accusation of wrongdoing against them, so it is a verb synonym.

clue.text: To talk foolishly is as expensive as it gets

parts.note: to prate is to chatter on at length about nothing

explanation.surface: Idle chatter is said to be the costliest thing there is.
explanation.definitionFit: The top rate of a charge or tax is the highest level, so it describes the most costly band there is.

clue.text: Make it compulsory to be in green for ceremony

indicators.note: the answer is said to be found within the next words, so its letters sit across them

explanation.surface: A rule is made that everyone must wear green for some ceremony.
explanation.definitionFit: To enforce a rule is to insist it is obeyed, which makes it obligatory in practice.

clue.text: Cap left off copy

indicators.note: the letter for left is taken off the word for cap

parts.note: a cap is a limit or limitation, as on spending

explanation.surface: A forged hat has had its left side removed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cap' looks like a hat but is a ceiling on amounts, LIMITATION; taking off L leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An imitation is something made to resemble another thing, so it is a noun synonym of copy.

clue.text: Potential fruit to ape backing instrument

parts.note: orang is a short form of orang-utan, a great ape

indicators.note: backing says the word for instrument is turned round to read from its end

parts.note: a pipe is a simple wind instrument

explanation.surface: Someone wants a fruit to imitate a backing instrument in a band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns the instrument round. 'to ape' looks like a verb meaning imitate, but 'ape' is a noun here.
explanation.definitionFit: A seed of a citrus fruit could grow into a tree bearing fruit, so it is fruit in potential.

clue.text: Cast having maybe final party

definitions.meaning: to cast is to throw or hurl
a last ... is a final bout of fun before settling down

explanation.definitionFit: To fling is to throw, and a fling is also a spell of wild enjoyment, often one's last.

clue.text: Bird digesting first of the article "Join the Navy"?

indicators.note: the bird is swallowing a letter, so the letter goes inside the bird's name

parts.note: a goose is a large waterbird

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the following word is taken

parts.note: a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A bird has eaten the first part of an article titled with a recruiting slogan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'digesting' puts T, from 'first of the', inside GOOSE to give GOTOSE, then A follows.
explanation.definitionFit: To take up a life as a sailor is the idiom, which joining a navy amounts to; the question mark flags it as an example.

clue.text: Tune with low notes heard at aviation centre

parts.note: an air is a melody

indicators.note: the clue says the low notes are heard, so a word that sounds like them is used

parts.note: bass is the lowest range of musical notes

explanation.surface: A melody with deep notes is played at an airport.
explanation.definitionFit: An air base is a military airfield, a centre for flying operations.

clue.text: See 16
Swill was in place of art for the moralist painter

indicators.note: the letters of was go where the letters of art stood, a straight swap

parts.note: William Hogarth painted moral series such as A Rake's Progress

explanation.surface: Pig feed was used instead of art by a moralising painter.
explanation.walkthrough: Hogarth was an 18th-century English painter of satirical moral tales. Replacing ART in his name with WAS gives HOG-WAS-H.
explanation.definitionFit: Hogwash is literally kitchen slop fed to pigs, the same as swill, and figuratively nonsense.

clue.text: Fool playing with clue for toga

parts.note: read the answer as wordplay: the second word rearranged spells toga, the first word being the anagram signal

explanation.surface: A joker toys with a crossword clue whose answer is a Roman garment.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse anagram: 'giddy' is a classic anagram signal and its fodder rearranges into TOGA, so the answer is itself a clue for toga.
explanation.definitionFit: To play the giddy goat is a British idiom for acting the fool, so the phrase stands for fooling about.

clue.text: To facilitate predation, dodgy mate's gone cheetah spotting

indicators.note: dodgy means unreliable or not right, so the following letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A big cat's partner has gone off spotting prey, all to help the hunt.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram 'dodgy' works on all 24 letters of MATES GONE CHEETAH SPOTTING, the S of 'mate's' included.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to stir up trouble, literally to put a predator among its prey.

clue.text: Gray, say, and keeping of the law in Latin

indicators.note: one word holds on to the other, so the second goes inside the first

parts.note: et is Latin for and, the closing 'in Latin' covering this word too
legis is the Latin genitive of lex, law, meaning of the law

explanation.surface: Something about a grey thing and how Latin keeps the law.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Gray wrote 'Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard'. 'in Latin' serves both pieces: ET (and) holds LEGIS (of the law).
explanation.definitionFit: Gray is the classic example of a writer of a mournful poem, and the clue's 'say' marks him as an example.

clue.text: Facilitate predation by forgetfulness about time to do good — be very angry with minister and model

indicators.note: the word for forgetfulness goes about, around, the letter for time

parts.note: Lethe is the river of forgetfulness in Greek myth
taken as written
to seethe is to be furious
a rabbi is a Jewish religious minister
the Model T was an early Ford car

explanation.surface: Someone forgets, then means well, then rages at a clergyman and a fashion model.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts T inside LETHE to give LETTHE. 'to' and 'with', 'and' are links between the many pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to give someone a fair chance, as a hunting dog is allowed sight of its quarry.

clue.text: Magistrate's poems accepted by parents and teachers

indicators.note: the poems are taken in by the parents and teachers, so they go inside

parts.note: PTA is a Parent-Teacher Association
odes are lyric poems

explanation.surface: A magistrate's poetry is welcomed by the school's parents and staff.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after 'Magistrate' stands for 'is', a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A podesta was a chief magistrate in medieval Italian city-states.

clue.text: Society attendant who is wool-gathering?

parts.note: a hearer is someone in attendance at a talk or sermon, a listener

explanation.surface: An attendant at a society function is caught daydreaming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wool-gathering' usually means daydreaming, but here it is literal: one who gathers the wool from sheep.
explanation.definitionFit: A shearer cuts the fleece off sheep, so the question-marked phrase is a literal reading of an idiom.

clue.text: I say none's up there where crime takes place

parts.note: at gives a location, answering where
a heist is a robbery

explanation.surface: Someone claims there is nobody upstairs where a robbery takes place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes place' is a link: the crime happens at a heist.
explanation.definitionFit: An unbeliever denies that any god exists in heaven, which is what the speaker of the phrase is saying.

clue.text: Queer street where shooting takes place

parts.note: a range is a place for target shooting

explanation.surface: An odd street where gunfire happens.
explanation.definitionFit: Queer in its old sense means odd or peculiar, a synonym of the answer.

clue.text: Tongue supplied to shoes

indicators.note: read as 'made supple', so the letters are worked loose and reformed

explanation.surface: A tongue is fitted to a pair of shoes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tongue' looks like part of a shoe; it means a language.
explanation.definitionFit: Sesotho is the Bantu language of Lesotho, so it is a tongue in the sense of a language.

clue.text: Rude letter about new thing Fenland rivers presumably do

indicators.note: the rude letter goes round, about, the abbreviation for new

parts.note: EP is an abbreviation for epistle, a letter

explanation.surface: A rude letter about something new is described.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts N inside RUDEEP. The Fens are flat eastern English marshland with slow, still rivers, and 'still waters run deep' is the proverb.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says still waters go to great depth, and the sluggish Fen rivers are presumed to be such still waters.

clue.text: See 16
Girl or county (you can tell which in Welsh)

indicators.text: you can tell which in Welsh
indicators.note: the bracket admits that only a Welsh speaker hears the girl's name and the county's as different, so to others they sound alike

parts.note: Gwynedd is a county in north-west Wales

explanation.surface: Someone is unsure if a name belongs to a girl or a county, which a Welsh speaker could settle.
explanation.walkthrough: In Welsh DD is voiced, as in 'the', and TH unvoiced, as in 'thin', so the names differ there; in English mouths they are much the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Gwyneth is a Welsh female first name, so it is an example of a girl's name.

clue.text: Church gathering cut short by way of joint lubricant

indicators.note: the word for the gathering loses its last letter, shortening it

parts.note: a synod is an assembly of church clergy
via means by way of

explanation.surface: A church meeting ended early, perhaps due to someone's sore joints.
explanation.definitionFit: Synovia is the fluid lubricating joints such as the knee, so it is that lubricant.

clue.text: The Third Man's girl had the lot in Sixth

indicators.note: the word for the lot sits in the Roman numeral for sixth

parts.note: VI is the Roman numeral for six
all means the lot, everything

explanation.surface: The girlfriend in a film had everything in the sixth form.
explanation.walkthrough: Alida Valli played Anna, Harry Lime's girlfriend, in the 1949 film The Third Man.
explanation.definitionFit: Alida Valli was the actress who played the female lead opposite Joseph Cotten and Orson Welles in that film.

clue.text: Display of sanctity by medieval bishop at Biblical city

parts.note: Odo was Bishop of Bayeux, half-brother of William the Conqueror
Ur of the Chaldees was Abraham's home city

explanation.surface: A medieval bishop shows his holiness at an Old Testament city.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'odour of sanctity' describes the sweet smell said to come from a saint's body.
explanation.definitionFit: In the set phrase about holiness, the smell is the outward sign, so the word stands for a display of it.

clue.text: Pregnant and not blackballed?

definitions.meaning: expecting a baby, in British slang
a candidate not voted out with a black ball is admitted to membership

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is British slang for expecting a baby, and literally means being a member of a society.

clue.text: As wet as it gets at 10 in planet — put finger out

indicators.note: the letters for at and ten go in the planet's name

parts.note: Saturn is the sixth planet
taken as written
the figures 1 and 0 look like the letters I and O
to point is to extend a finger at something

explanation.surface: Something reaches maximum dampness at ten on a planet, and someone points.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' places the two short pieces just before the planet's final letter; reading 10 as I and O is a visual trick.
explanation.definitionFit: Saturation point is the state where nothing can absorb any more liquid, the maximum of wetness.
